intro: A stately opening, a scurrying tune and a crescendo that keeps finding another gear. Fritz Reiner and the Chicago Symphony Orchestra play the overture that Rossini put to work in three different operas.

cues.title: A stately opening
cues.text: The introduction moves slowly in E major. Loud orchestral chords interrupt the quieter phrases; the music makes a great ceremony of getting ready.
cues.evidence: Ricordi full score, reprinted by Dover, pp. 1–4: Andante maestoso in E major, with forte and fortissimo chords between quieter phrases. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/c/c8/IMSLP517981-PMLP7237-Rossini_-_Il_barbiere_di_Siviglia_-_Act_I_(orch._score)_(etc).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The quick minor-key tune
cues.text: The Allegro vivo starts in E minor, with quick, light string figures. Rossini makes room for woodwind solos between the orchestral bursts.
cues.evidence: Ricordi full score, reprinted by Dover, p. 4 onwards: Allegro vivo in E minor, following a held rest; the opening melody is shared by piccolo, first violins and violas. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/c/c8/IMSLP517981-PMLP7237-Rossini_-_Il_barbiere_di_Siviglia_-_Act_I_(orch._score)_(etc).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three operas, one overture
cues.text: Before Figaro acquired this overture, it opened Aureliano in Palmira in 1813 and Elisabetta, regina d’Inghilterra in 1815. Two serious operas supplied the curtain-raiser for a comedy.
cues.evidence: IMSLP’s work catalogue traces the overture from Aureliano in Palmira through the revised Elisabetta version to Il barbiere di Siviglia. https://imslp.org/wiki/Il_barbiere_di_Siviglia_(Rossini,_Gioachino)

cues.title: The major-key finish
cues.text: The ending settles firmly in E major. Short figures repeat, the orchestra grows louder, and the cadence receives one emphatic reinforcement after another.
cues.evidence: Ricordi full score, reprinted by Dover, pp. 20–22: Più mosso, E major, repeated cadential figures and the final tonic chord. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/c/c8/IMSLP517981-PMLP7237-Rossini_-_Il_barbiere_di_Siviglia_-_Act_I_(orch._score)_(etc).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.value: Rossini’s underlying composition is out of copyright under ordinary life-plus-70 terms.
fields.note: Rossini died in 1868. The overture originated in Aureliano in Palmira in 1813 and was reused in Elisabetta in 1815 and Barber in 1816. This assessment does not clear unidentified modern editions.

fields.note: Selected under the project’s eu-published-before-1963 rule. The pre-extension fifty-year term had expired before 1 November 2013. This is not a worldwide public-domain claim, a Creative Commons licence, or a claim that the 1959 recording is out of copyright in the United States.

composer.epithet: He made a roomful of quarrelling people sing like clockwork, then gave William Tell an orchestra of mountains and storms.
facts: Lugo with Giuseppe Malerbi; Bologna Liceo Musicale from 1806, including counterpoint with Stanislao Mattei
Venice and Milan · Naples under Domenico Barbaja · Rome · Théâtre-Italien and Opéra, Paris

quote.text: I was born for comic opera, as you well know!
quote.source: Rossini addressing God in the manuscript of his Petite messe solennelle (1863); our translation from the French.

composer.background:
On 20 February 1816, at Rome’s Teatro Argentina, a barber came on stage announcing that everyone needed him. Figaro could shave a chin, deliver a letter and arrange a marriage; his repeated calls of his own name threatened to exhaust even his singer. The opera was advertised as Almaviva, ossia L’inutile precauzione. Its first night failed. Within a few performances the public had changed its mind, and Rossini’s Barber of Seville was on its way.

Gioachino Rossini was born in Pesaro on 29 February 1792. His father Giuseppe played horn and trumpet; his mother Anna Guidarini became a professional singer. The boy travelled with their work. In Lugo, from 1802, the priest Giuseppe Malerbi taught him composition and introduced him to Haydn and Mozart. At Bologna’s Liceo Musicale, which he entered in 1806, Rossini studied cello, piano and counterpoint. Before he was an opera composer he had been a theatre musician, a singer and a player at the keyboard.
